Miguel Angel Asturias. A Guatemalan novelist, poet, and diplomat whose work draws on Mayan mythology and the political violence of Central America to create hallucinatory, dreamlike fictions that blur the boundary between realism and the mythic. Living from eighteen ninety-nine to nineteen seventy-four, Asturias was a pioneer of magical realism before the term was coined, using indigenous Mesoamerican thought and surrealist technique to expose dictatorship, colonialism, and the dispossession of indigenous peoples.

His masterwork El Señor Presidente, published in nineteen forty-six, is a baroque, nightmarish novel set in an unnamed Central American dictatorship. It depicts surveillance, torture, and paranoia through fragmented, hallucinatory prose that mirrors the protagonist's psychological dissolution. Three years later came Men of Maize, an experimental novel drawing on Mayan creation mythology and the relationship between indigenous peoples and the land, employing non-linear narrative and indigenous Quiche perspectives.

Asturias was influenced by surrealism and his study of Mayan texts and culture—his work is steeped in indigenous mythology and the history of indigenous dispossession. He served as ambassador and diplomat, representing Guatemala internationally while remaining engaged with its political turmoil and the struggle for indigenous rights. In nineteen sixty-seven he won the Nobel Prize in Literature, awarded for his vivid literary achievement, rooted in strong national traits and individual authorial inventiveness.

As a pioneer of magical realism in Latin American letters, Asturias's formal innovations and engagement with magical realism anticipated and influenced Garcia Marquez's later work. His blend of the mythic and political became a model for the movement itself. He remains Guatemala's greatest writer and a central voice in Central American letters, his work centering indigenous Mesoamerican culture and the history of colonial violence.
